speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: asked the Minister for Home Affairs in light of the case of a foreign preacher who entered Singapore using a passport with a different name, what are the lessons learnt to increase border security, including the usage of biometric data or other technological tools.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: asked the Minister for Home Affairs in light of the recent case of a foreign preacher delivering an illegal sermon in a dormitory in Tuas, what are the rules governing the use of foreign worker dormitories for events involving speakers or religious preachers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: asked the Minister for Home Affairs (a) how effective are the measures deployed by the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority to detect and prevent undesirable travellers from entering Singapore by using a valid passport but with a different name; and (b) how prevalent have such attempts been made in the past three years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: asked the Minister for Home Affairs whether the Bangladeshi religious preacher who entered and delivered a sermon in Singapore on 9 August 2024 is on any watchlist in the possession of Home Team security agencies.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: The questions are from Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Neil Parekh, Mr Melvin Yong, Mr Ang Wei Neng, Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim and Mr Pritam Singh.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My reply will also address a similar question raised by Mr Sharael Taha1 for a subsequent Sitting.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In his sermon, he made statements which were extremist and segregationist.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He left Singapore next day, on 10 August 2024.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members have raised a number of questions, whether Amir Hamza was on the watchlist of the security agencies and, more broadly, the way in which persons come through Singapore’s borders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are a number of steps taken at our borders, as many Members will be aware.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Nationals of some countries are required to apply for visas even before they come in – Bangladesh is one such country.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Applications from those on our watchlist or otherwise raise some questions, will usually be rejected.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All travellers are also required to submit an SG Arrival Card before arriving in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) uses that information, other information it receives and information from advance passenger lists from airlines, including flight manifests, and other sources of information, to conduct a pre-arrival risk assessment of the travellers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When the travellers come into Singapore, they are screened against a watchlist of persons, even as they undergo immigration clearance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Those on the watchlist or are identified to be of higher risk by ICA’s backend data analytics will be checked further.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: ICA officers also look out for persons' reasons for visiting Singapore that may appear dubious or for other reasons that may require further checking, and these travellers might be required to undergo further checks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In July 2020, we also introduced the Multi-Modal Biometric System.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First-time visitors will have their facial, iris and fingerprint images captured at immigration clearance, and that allows us to better detect repeat visitors who may try and come in using multiple identities or impersonated identities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For foreign visitors, this is usually done on the first occasion they visit Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our automated gates are generally able to detect forged passports as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In all, for various reasons, about 2,500 visitors are refused entry at our checkpoints every month.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Internal Security Department (ISD) had put him on the watchlist and that is because he had made statements promoting religious intolerance and for a few other reasons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He applied for a visa to enter Singapore using a passport with a name that was different from what we had in our database and therefore, that other name was not our watchlist.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And he used that passport on 9 August to come into Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As this was his first visit to Singapore, we did not have his biometrics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If he tries to come back again, regardless of what other passports he uses, he will be picked up because we now have his biometrics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members have asked questions, broadly, about the security at our borders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are about 600,000 travellers every day coming and going across all our checkpoints.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members will appreciate – we have to develop a framework for picking up some people of concern while allowing the vast majority to clear as quickly as possible.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We need to strike a balance between security and facilitation at our borders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not possible nor practicable to subject every visitor, obviously, to stringent, detailed checks and interviews.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: No country has a comprehensive database of every criminal or person of security concern across the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Certainly, Singapore does not have such a database.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, in summary, in terms of persons coming in, the majority of persons who are perceived to have dubious reasons or purposes for coming into Singapore are picked up either through the visa scheme or even without visas, through other information that we have at various levels.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And as I have said, about 2,500 are rejected every month – some of them with visas, some of them without visas.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it is always possible that a small number will get through despite the several levels of checks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members must also understand that the levels of checks and our information-gathering varies depending on the type and extent of risks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Obviously, ISD together with its foreign counterparts will have a closer awareness of persons who may want to do us physical harm in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will not go into operational considerations, but there are a number of ways in which those persons would be picked up more easily.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: No system is foolproof, but there are different levels of checks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members have also asked about the rules and regulations governing events at migrant worker dormitories and the actions the Government has taken to ensure that dormitory operators comply.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Public Order Act requires event organisers to apply for a Police permit for cause-based events that are open to the public.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The speech at the dormitory would be one such event.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It applies to events involving religious teachings, regardless of whether the event takes place within a dormitory or elsewhere.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Specifically for foreign worker dormitories, the Foreign Employee Dormitories Act imposes licence conditions that require operators to keep updated records of all non-residents, including visitors or contractors, who enter the living areas of the dormitories.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Ministry of Manpower consults relevant agencies, including ISD, in its assessment when such applications are received.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant asked how often such illegal events occur within our migrant worker dormitories.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Based on our records and assessments, this sort of event does not usually take place.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is very rare because somebody will have to be actively in breach of all of these requirements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And of course, if we detect it, swift action will be taken.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will continue to educate and remind our dormitory operators to ensure that they obtain the relevant approvals before conducting such activities in the dormitories.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And of course, our best safeguard is a public that stays vigilant and reports these sorts of individuals and activities to the agencies.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister explain how MHA is committed to continue adopting artificial intelligence (AI) or new technologies like gait recognition technology, the way we walk, or reverse facial recognition tools to detect someone?
But for context, do Bangladeshi nationals visiting Singapore require visas and letters of introduction (LOIs) from a local contact here and also go through a list of authorised visa agents there?

Given this incident, would MHA investigate the local contact on the LOI issued, review the process of the list of authorised visa agents and perhaps require biometric data to be provided and review, generally speaking, the process for visa applications?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the first question, we have to use technology, and we are using technology and people have gone through our borders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We see increasingly more and more technology being introduced; multimodal biometric is one example.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For foreigners, once they enrol, they can also use the systems.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We want to make the airport and checkpoint experience smooth because, remember, the vast majority of persons who are coming into Singapore are coming in for business, tourist or social reasons, for valid purposes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we cannot make their experience a difficult one.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, this is what I meant by balance between security and Singapore's economy, well-being and as a welcoming place for tourists and others who are coming into Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A very small number come with bad intentions and our systems have so far been robust enough to pick most of them up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Zhulkarnain spoke about gait and movements, those are all items, part of data that have long been used.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are technologies, there are techniques, it is some sort of science, and we work with other agencies across the world to study these and train our officers on these.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With regard to the visa application process, I seek the Minister's confirmation whether a photograph also was required to be submitted by the preacher in the course of his visa application and whether there are particular processes by which that individual, as he is pictorially represented or represented in the picture, is cross-checked with the watchlist.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And if there is no such process, can the Minister confirm whether, beyond my supplementary question, improvements are being considered to capture individuals who are already existing on a watchlist and clearly present a different level of threat, as compared to the average person who walks through our immigration gates?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Photographs, I believe, were submitted, I have not checked on this case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The normal process would be that it would be cross-checked against the watchlist.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It depends on the type of photograph that is submitted and the quality of the photograph.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It may not always pick up against the database that we have and, without going into details, I think the Member also assumes that in our database, there will be photographs of all those who are listed in the watchlist.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sometimes, we will only have names without photographs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As for the ability to cross-check, my understanding is that our systems are very advanced and if there is a broad match in the photographs, they would have picked it up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the question assumes that we had a photograph to cross-check against.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While automation and biometrics are vital in modern immigration processes, there may be concerns about over-reliance on technology.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on the rationale behind the current level of automation and how does it ensure that human judgement remains integral in identifying potential threats?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Every single person, the 600,000 persons who are crossing our borders, will then have to be checked individually.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I think Members can appreciate that we might as well take a big hit on our economic sector.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I think the Member's real question is to what extent is technology supplemented by the assessment by our officers and that is a fair question.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They help us but, in the end, there is also an assessment by officers on selected and specific cases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are also officers at the various checkpoints assessing people as they are walking through, going through and some are picked up for additional checks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some are picked up based on information or documents submitted, while some are picked up based on our assessment of the individuals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And there have been a number of cases where the visas do not throw up anything and the passports are fine, but our officers, through their training, are able to assess that some individuals require further checks and quite often, that throws up persons who are carrying contraband, bringing in drugs or otherwise coming in with intentions that we do not agree with.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Minister's response covered Parliamentary Question Nos 2 to 8 in today's Order Paper.
